title: Why falsifiability separates empirical science from dogma
dek: How Karl Popper argued that scientific theories must specify observations that could prove them wrong.
sentences: Many people believe that scientific knowledge advances simply by gathering evidence that confirms an existing theoretical hypothesis.
However, philosopher Karl Popper observed that confirming evidence is remarkably easy to find if one is actively looking for confirmation.
A theory that explains every conceivable outcome explains nothing at all, because no possible observation can challenge it.
Popper argued that the genuine hallmark of scientific inquiry is not verification, but falsifiability.
A scientific statement must be capable of being shown false by a possible empirical observation or experimental test.
If a theory cannot specify under what observable circumstances it would be mistaken, it belongs to pseudoscience or dogma.
Albert Einstein exemplified this principle by declaring that if starlight did not bend around the sun during an eclipse, general relativity was false.
When a falsifiable prediction survives rigorous empirical testing, the theory gains provisional scientific credibility without being permanently proven.
Scientific progress occurs not by accumulating absolute certainties, but by systematically eliminating hypotheses that fail severe tests.
Science remains an open and self-correcting discipline precisely because every accepted truth remains open to empirical challenge.
The strength of a scientific idea lies in its vulnerability to experimental refutation rather than rhetorical defense.

keyPoints.statement: A theory is scientific only if it makes predictions that could be shown false by empirical observation.
keyPoints.addHint: Define Popper's criterion of falsifiability: a scientific theory must make risky predictions that empirical observation could prove false.
keyPoints.example: Popper argued that for a theory to be scientific, it must make specific claims that could be shown false by empirical testing.

keyPoints.statement: Theories gain credibility by surviving attempts at refutation, but they remain provisional rather than proven with absolute certainty.
keyPoints.addHint: Explain provisional acceptance: theories gain credibility when they survive tests that could have disproved them, but they are never absolute proof.
keyPoints.example: Theories that survive rigorous attempts to disprove them gain provisional credibility, but they never reach absolute permanent certainty.

keyPoints.statement: Science progresses through error elimination and self-correction, not by seeking confirmation for unfalsifiable claims.
keyPoints.addHint: Describe scientific progress: science moves forward by eliminating flawed hypotheses rather than simply collecting easy confirmations.
keyPoints.example: Scientific progress happens by weeding out hypotheses that fail tests, keeping the discipline open to correction.

commonMisconceptions.statement: A theory that explains every possible outcome is the most scientific theory
commonMisconceptions.why: Popper showed that a theory that explains everything cannot be tested or falsified, making it unscientific.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A theory that explains every conceivable outcome is unfalsifiable and therefore unscientific, not superior.

commonMisconceptions.statement: Surviving experimental tests proves a scientific theory with 100 percent certainty
commonMisconceptions.why: Surviving tests confers provisional acceptance; future tests could still refute the theory.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Surviving empirical tests gives a theory provisional credibility; science never claims 100 percent certainty.

samples.label: Clear explanation
samples.text: The article outlines Karl Popper's argument that falsifiability defines genuine empirical science. Confirming evidence is easy to find when actively sought, and theories that explain every imaginable outcome explain nothing because they risk nothing. Popper argued that a statement is scientific only if it specifies observations that could prove it false. Einstein demonstrated this by stating general relativity would fail if starlight did not bend around the sun. When falsifiable theories survive rigorous tests, they earn provisional credibility, though science never claims absolute certainty. Progress happens through error elimination.

samples.label: Contains a misconception
samples.text: A theory that explains every possible outcome is the most scientific theory possible because it cannot be wrong. When an experiment supports a theory, that proves the theory with 100 percent certainty as absolute permanent truth that nobody can ever question again.
